newsitem.title: USA: Fed seen holding interest rates steady -- for now.
newsitem.headline: Fed seen holding interest rates steady -- for now.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Despite news that the U.S. economy ended 1996 with a bang, the Federal Reserve is widely expected to hold interest rates steady at a two-day meeting that starts on Tuesday.
With inflation quiescent and, by at least by one measure, at a 30-year low, the central bank has scant justification for raising short-term rates now, economists said.
"Inflation is looking very well-behaved," David Seiders, chief economist at the National Association of Home Builders, said. "They would be hard pressed to make a move now."
The government reported on Friday that the economy grew at a torrid annualized pace of 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter. But the rapid growth failed to fire up inflation.

Still, many analysts believe it is only a matter of time before the Fed raises interest rates. With the job market taut and wages showing signs of picking up, the central bank will need to tigten credit a notch if it wants to keep inflation in check, they said.

"The Fed will be trigger-finger ready to raise interest rates when and if inflation looks like it will get over 3 percent," said Allen Sinai, chief global economist for Boston-based Primark Decision Economics Inc.
Twenty-five of 26 private economists polled by Reuters forecast that the central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee will decide to stand pat this week.
But 17 of those same analysts predict a rate increase sometime this year, perhaps as early as March.
The Fed has held rates steady for over a year, since cutting them by a quarter percentage point on Jan. 31, 1996.
The federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for loans now stands at 5.25 percent. The discount rate the Fed charges on its loans to the banks is 5 percent.
In testimony to Congress last month, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan painted a picture of an economy that was surprisingly free of imbalances and inflationary pressures six years into expansion.
But he warned of the risk that inflation could pick up as workers take advantage of the tight jobs market to demand much higher wages and benefits from their employers.

So far that has not happened. While wage growth has picked up, companies have been able to hold down their overall labour bill thanks to subdued rises in health care benefits. But Fed officials said that can only last so long.

"Inflation is not here yet, but it could go up down the road because of healthy economic growth coupled with tight labour markets," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Minneapolis-based Norwest Corp.
He said that the economy's rapid growth in the final three months was much faster than the Fed wants because it is not sustainable on long-term basis without fanning inflation.

At their meeting this week, Fed policymakers are scheduled to discuss their projections for economic growth, inflation and unemployment this year for presentation by Greenspan to Congress later this month.

Several Fed policymakers have already said publicly that they expect moderate economic growth this year in the 2 percent to 2-1/2 percent range. On a fourth quarter on fourth quarter basis, the economy grew by 3.4 percent last year.

But Chris Varvares, President of Macroeconomic Advisers of St. Louis, said there is a risk that inflation will pick up this year even if growth moderates because the economy is already running at such high level of capacity.

That eventually may prove enough to convince the Fed to take out some "monetary insurance" and raise interest rates a notch. But that will not happen until it can draw a better bead on where the economy -- and inflation -- is headed, he said.
